text: The efficient-market hypothesis says prices reflect available information, so investors should not consistently earn risk-adjusted excess returns. | Event studies often show rapid reactions to public news, although some returns drift after announcements. | Size, value, momentum, and reversal challenge simple efficiency, but they do not guarantee profitable trading rules. | Every efficiency test is joint with an asset-pricing model. Abnormal returns can reflect mispricing or a misspecified risk benchmark. | Markets become more efficient when active traders exploit anomalies. Risk, trading costs, and publication can erode the returns. | 41 | Final synthesis | Sources: Fama (1970); Fama & French (1992, 1998); Jegadeesh & Titman (1993); De Bondt & Thaler (1985); Grossman & Stiglitz (1980); McLean & Pontiff (2016).
